data.content_ref: inline:SRC_002's central criterion for distinguishing genuine reliability gain from mere compliance within a single evaluation relies on the variance of panel members' individual judgments: low variance allegedly indicates proxy-based compliance forcing agreement, while genuine preservation of the expert's decision structure produces variance. But this prediction lacks a causal mechanism: SRC_002 never explains *why* a checklist that preserves the expert's causal structure would yield higher inter-member variance. The disanalogy SRC_002 itself notes — that a shared checklist forces perfectly correlated errors if flawed — implies the checklist constrains all members identically, so variance reflects the protocol's interpretive ambiguity, not whether the checklist captures the generative mechanism. A checklist encoding the true causal features could still be applied deterministically, yielding zero variance; conversely, a flawed proxy checklist could produce high variance if items are ambiguous. SRC_002 thus cannot show that high variance is the signature of genuine structural preservation rather than of ambiguous proxy wording.
